newsitem.title: UK: Europe's high yield bonds close on US, risks loom.
newsitem.headline: Europe's high yield bonds close on US, risks loom.

text.p: Yields on some of Europe's "high yield" bonds have dipped below U.S. Treasuries, prompting fears their success is balanced too finely on a successful European monetary union rather than fundamentals.
"You have to ask where the demand is going to come from for these previously high yielders when they're yielding less than Treasuries," said CSFB economist Sean Shepley on Wednesday.
"And I guess the answer is, as long as people are convinced interest rates in those countries are going to come down, you can still find a demand for them on a momentum basis."

Spanish, Italian and Swedish bonds, renowned for offering high rewards to risk-happy investors, have seen yields squeezed gradually closer to German Bunds by converging interest rates in the run-up to European economic and monetary union (EMU). Now the market is rating some of these bonds as safe as U.S. debt.
Spanish 10-year Bonos yield 6.67 percent, against 6.66 percent for U.S. 10-years. Swedish 10-year debt does not yield much more at 6.83 percent while Italian 10-years are at 7.20.

Italian bonds are seen as among the most vulnerable. Given the country's historically weak currency and unstable political background, some investors say this situation hangs too heavily on the realisation of EMU.

"The whole EMU process could quite easily falter, and the risks are certainly building," said Jeremy Cunningham, of Robert Fleming International bond fund. "This close to the end date, the effect of any slight hitch will be more profound."

The uptrend in Italian BTPs began in early 1995 as EMU-driven fiscal reform began and inflation started to fall. As confidence in EMU grew through 1996, the BTP/Bund spread has tightened and the Italian market now demands smaller premiums than in the traditionally safer British gilt market.
"Why shouldn't they have lower yields?" said a fixed income head in Copenhagen. "They've improved dramatically on their debt and budget deficits and are in a very favourable situation."
But some say without the EMU factor, T-notes would strongly outperform these bonds. Some chartists have also said the Italian market, for one, is overbought and ripe for a setback.
One London economist said it was mainly domestic investors driving the former high-yielding markets forward, with many foreigners increasingly neutral or underweight there.

He said the markets had also been pushed up by the decline in new debt issues as budget deficits were reduced to meet the Maastricht criteria. This drop in supply effectively increased demand, which pushed prices up.

Many expect EMU to go ahead on January 1, 1999 with a core group of members. Convergence criteria include long-term interest rates, stipulating a country's government debt must yield no more than two percentage points above the three best performing countries.

J.P. Morgan's EMU calculator, which is based on bond yield spreads in the swaps market, recently put the probability of Sweden joining the first wave of entrants at 73 percent and Italy at 74. It gave Spain 79 percent - after France and Belgium at 100 percent.
This is despite economic forecasts, which show all three countries are likely to fail EMU's debt and deficit criteria.

Paul Meader, managing director at Rothschilds Bank Switzerland, predicted volatility ahead. "It's going to be a slightly bumpier ride until the year end, but there is plenty of potential for the convergence process to continue."
He agreed with other analysts that European markets were expensive in relation to the United States.

"With every day the curve narrows, the risk-reward is slowly starting to shift against you," said Meader. "There isn't a lot of protection for any swing in sentiment against the convergence process and against the idea of EMU occurring on time."
He said investors were well protected when yields were 250 basis points over Bunds, as fundamentals in Italy and Spain justified such spreads regardless of the convergence process.

Although Meader said he would stick his neck on the block and predict 10-year BTPs at 50 over Bunds and bonos 20 over by year end, he saw few reasons aside from EMU to hold these bonds without that protective yield buffer.
He added that the narrowing spreads could lead to weaker currencies against the mark, making the risk-reward tradeoff even less attractive in total return terms.
